newsitem.title: TURKEY: France and allies at odds on north Iraq patrols.
newsitem.headline: France and allies at odds on north Iraq patrols.

text.p: France on Wednesday held back support for a U.S.-led bid to keep President Saddam Hussein out of northern Iraq in a sign of a fresh rift between NATO allies Paris and Washington.
Talks in Turkey on the future of a no-fly zone imposed on Baghdad in the north hit a serious snag when France opposed planned changes to Western allied monitoring flights, Turkish officials said.
"France made it known this afternoon that it was not ready for an agreement on technical issues at the moment," a Turkish foreign ministry official told Reuters.
Washington and Ankara had agreed to alter a U.S., British and French air force that patrols northern Iraq from a base in Turkey.
"French authorities will study the new conditions created by this decision and will make their position known at the right time," a French foreign ministry spokesman said in Paris.

Despite news of the row, the Turkish parliament backed the changes by legally ending the current operation, known as Provide Comfort, on December 31 and backing its replacement with similar flights in the new year.
The planes have been shielding Iraq's Kurds from Baghdad since hundreds of thousands of people fled to Turkey and Iran after a failed Kurdish uprising at the end of the 1991 Gulf War.
The nature of France's objections were not immediately clear. A Western diplomatic source in Turkey said Paris might pull out of the air force. "It seems like they won't participate," he said.

France and the United States have been at odds this month over the U.S. command of NATO forces in southern Europe, French objections to the appointment of U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan and an alleged high-level diplomatic snub.
France supplies about half a dozen planes to the northern Iraq contingent of some 50 aircraft.
The allied force's ground command centre in the northern Iraqi town of Zakho was scrapped after Saddam gained a foothold in the region in inter-Kurdish fighting in the summer.

A mention of France as a member of future air operations in the region was deleted at the last minute from a draft law on the force presented to the Turkish parliament, deputy speaker Kamer Genc said.
MPs voted 255 to 217 to give Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's government the power to authorise new air probes into northern Iraq after the New Year's Eve deadline runs out.
"There is still a need for Iraq to be monitored closely," Defence Minister Turhan Tayan told a parliamentary debate.
Under pressure from the Turkish military, Islamist Erbakan has gone back on promises to throw the force out of Turkey.
The United States has abandoned its aid, intelligence and military operations in northern Iraq in the face of Baghdad's increased influence in the region.
Iraqi troops and tanks helped a Kurdish faction capture Kurds capital city from a rival group on August 31, prompting retaliatory U.S. cruise missile strikes on Iraqi targets.
France temporarily pulled out of the operation in September after the U.S. missile attacks.
Paris, eager to help exploit Iraqi oil resources, has courted Baghdad's favour and pressed for an end to United Nations sanctions against Iraq.
